title: Indian National Movement
summary: ## Rise of nationalism

The Renaissance and the French Revolution (Liberty, Equality, Fraternity) spread nationalism in the world. In India it grew in the 19th century, after 1857, because of common oppression under colonial rule, political and administrative unity under one set of British laws, economic exploitation, the socio-religious reform movements, the printing press, and writers like Bankim Chandra Chatterji ('Vande Mataram', later banned by the British), Swami Dayanand and Aurobindo Ghosh. Vivekananda's call 'Arise, awake and stop not till the goal is reached' inspired people. Regional bodies such as the Indian Association and Poona Sarvajanik Sabha worked separately; the need for one national body led to the Indian National Congress.
## Indian National Congress and the Moderates (1885–1905)

A.O. Hume, a retired civil servant, founded the Congress in 1885 to give Indians a safe, constitutional outlet; Viceroy Dufferin supported him. Womesh Chandra Banerjee was the first President. Leaders such as Pherozeshah Mehta, Gokhale, Dadabhai Naoroji and Badruddin Tyabji had faith in British justice and used petitions — hence 'Moderates'. They asked for representative legislatures, Indianisation of services, ICS exams in India, less military spending, lower land revenue and salt duty, and help for Indian industries. They achieved little (Indian Councils Act 1892), but created national awakening and political training.
## Partition of Bengal (1905) and the Radicals

Lord Curzon, a staunch imperialist (Indian Universities Act 1904), partitioned Bengal in 1905, claiming better administration; the real aim was 'Divide and Rule' between Hindus and Muslims and weakening the movement in Bengal. Indians protested with meetings and processions, tied rakhis as a symbol of unity, and launched the Swadeshi and Boycott movements; Swadeshi mills, banks and stores were set up and students and women took part. The partition was annulled in 1911.

The Radicals or 'Garam Dal' — Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal) — felt the Moderates' methods were weak. They believed freedom was a right ('Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' — Tilak), and used mass protests, boycott and swadeshi. The Congress split in 1907; the two groups reunited at Lucknow in 1916 through Annie Besant, who started the Home Rule movement in 1914. The Lucknow Pact (1916) brought the Congress and Muslim League together to demand self-government.
## Muslim League and reforms

The All India Muslim League was founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906 (Aga Khan its President) to protect Muslim interests; it was the first fruit of the British policy of Divide and Rule. The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) enlarged the councils but gave them no real power and introduced separate electorates for Muslims. The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
## World War I and its aftermath

Indian leaders helped Britain in the war hoping for self-government, but heavy war loans, higher land revenue, forced recruitment, rising prices and new taxes caused unrest. The Khilafat Movement was started by Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali because the Ottoman Empire was broken up and the Khalifa insulted. The Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed arrest and imprisonment without trial. On 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, killing about a thousand; Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood.
## Gandhi and mass movements

Gandhi developed Satyagraha (non-violent insistence on truth) in South Africa, returned in 1915, founded the Sabarmati Ashram (1916) and led satyagrahas at Champaran (1917, indigo planters), Kheda (peasants hit by crop failure) and Ahmedabad (mill workers).

Non-Cooperation Movement (August 1920), merged with the Khilafat movement: surrender of titles, boycott of government schools, courts, councils and foreign goods; swadeshi, hand-spinning, removal of untouchability and Hindu–Muslim unity. Students, teachers and lawyers (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das) joined. After mob violence at Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922) Gandhi suspended it in February 1922. The Swaraj Party (C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, 1923) contested the councils. The all-white Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted with 'Simon Go Back'; Lala Lajpat Rai died after a police lathi charge. The Nehru Report outlined a constitution. At the Lahore session (1929) the Congress demanded Purna Swaraj and celebrated 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.

Civil Disobedience: Gandhi marched from Sabarmati to Dandi and broke the Salt Law on 6 April 1930; farmers, traders and women joined. The Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931) followed and Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference. The movement spread political awareness even to remote villages.
## Revolutionaries and socialists

Revolutionaries such as Khudiram Bose, Prafulla Chaki, V.D. Savarkar, Lala Hardayal (Ghadar Party), Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqullah Khan (Kakori, 1925), Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh (Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, 1928) used armed methods. Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8 April 1929 shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad'; Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged in 1931. The All India Trade Union Congress (1920) and leaders like Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose (who later formed the Forward Bloc) spread socialist ideas.
## Communal divide

Separate electorates (1909), their extension (1919), the Communal Award (1932) and the Act of 1935 hampered national unity. Jinnah put forward the two-nation theory and the demand for Pakistan (1940).
## Towards independence (1935–1947)

The Government of India Act 1935 proposed an All India Federation; provinces got autonomy but only 14% could vote. Congress won the 1937 elections and formed ministries in 7 of 11 provinces, but resigned in 1939 when India was dragged into World War II. Vinoba Bhave was the first individual satyagrahi (1940). The Cripps Mission (1942) offered only dominion status after the war and failed.

Subhas Chandra Bose escaped to Berlin (1941), took charge of the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) in 1943, gave the cries 'Chalo Dilli' and 'Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga', and the Indian flag was hoisted at Kohima in 1944.

Quit India Movement: passed at Wardha (14 July 1942) and Bombay (8 August 1942) with Gandhi's mantra 'Do or Die'. Leaders were arrested on 9 August; people attacked symbols of British rule, and parallel governments arose in Ballia, Midnapore and Satara. It showed that independence was no longer a matter of bargain.

The Cabinet Mission (1946) proposed a federal government; elections to the Constituent Assembly followed. The League observed 'Direct Action Day' (16 August 1946), leading to riots. Lord Mountbatten's plan (June 1947) accepted partition, and under the Indian Independence Act India became free on 15 August 1947, along with Pakistan.

vsa: Why did Mahatma Gandhi launch the Non-Cooperation Movement in August 1920? Explain.

The Rowlatt Act allowed imprisonment without trial and the government ignored Indian protests; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the injustice to the Khalifa (Khilafat issue) angered Indians. Gandhi felt no purpose was served by cooperating with such a government, so he asked people to withdraw cooperation non-violently.

or: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted by Indians? Give two reasons.

(1) It had no Indian member — it was an all-white commission deciding India's constitutional future. (2) Indians saw it as an insult and a denial of their right to self-government, so they protested with black flags and 'Simon Go Back'.

vsa: Why was the Khilafat Movement started?

During World War I Muslims supported the British on the understanding that the holy places of the Ottoman Empire would remain with the Khalifa. After the war the Ottoman Empire was divided and the Turkish Sultan (Khalifa) humiliated, so Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali started the Khilafat Movement.
What do you understand by 'Purna Swaraj'?
Purna Swaraj means complete independence and sovereignty. The Congress adopted it as its goal at the Lahore session of 1929 and celebrated 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.
Differentiate between the Moderates and the Radicals.

Moderates (1885–1905) had faith in British justice and placed demands through petitions within the law. Radicals (Lal-Bal-Pal) believed freedom was a right and used mass protests, boycott of foreign goods and swadeshi to involve the people.
Why did Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt throw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly?
On 8 April 1929 they threw it to protest against the passage of the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill and to awaken the people, shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad'; no one was hurt.
sa: Examine the significance of 'Vande Mataram' in the nationalist movement of India.

Bankim Chandra Chatterji's hymn to the Motherland became the rallying cry of patriotic nationalists. It inspired generations to supreme self-sacrifice and expressed love for the motherland. It created such fear among the British that they banned the song.

or: How did regional organisations turn into a national organisation during colonial India?

Many regional bodies such as the Indian Association, Bengal Presidency Association and Poona Sarvajanik Sabha raised voices against British rule separately. Leaders felt that joint work would make Indian demands stronger, which led to the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1885 as an all-India body.

sa: Describe the main features of the Dandi March.

(1) Gandhi opposed the tax on salt, a basic need of everyone. (2) In March–April 1930 he marched from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi on the Gujarat coast. (3) On 6 April 1930 he broke the Salt Law by picking up sea salt. (4) It was peaceful, and farmers, traders and women joined in large numbers; Gandhi was arrested in May 1930. It began the Civil Disobedience Movement.

How did the First World War influence India? Explain.

(1) Indian leaders supported Britain hoping for self-government after the war. (2) To repay war loans the British raised land revenue, increased prices, imposed income taxes and forcibly recruited soldiers, causing unrest. (3) Peasants and workers protested at Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad. (4) The Lucknow Pact and Home Rule movement strengthened the demand for self-rule, and the division of the Ottoman Empire led to the Khilafat Movement.

Who announced the Partition of Bengal? Describe its impact on Indian society.

Lord Curzon (1905). Impact: (1) Indians saw it as Divide and Rule and protested through meetings, processions and the press; Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis to show unity. (2) The Swadeshi and Boycott movements began; swadeshi mills, banks and stores were set up. (3) Students and women joined, the Radicals rose to prominence, and the partition was annulled in 1911.

Describe Mahatma Gandhi's programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).

(1) Surrender of titles and honorary offices and resignation from nominated seats. (2) Boycott of government schools and colleges, courts, legislative councils and foreign goods. (3) Refusal to attend official functions or join the army for service in Mesopotamia. (4) Constructive programme: swadeshi, hand-spinning and weaving, removal of untouchability and Hindu–Muslim unity.

Explain the role of revolutionaries and secret societies in the National Movement.

Angered by British repression, young revolutionaries formed secret societies in Punjab, Bengal, Maharashtra and UP. Khudiram Bose, Savarkar, Lala Hardayal (Ghadar Party), Bismil and Ashfaqullah (Kakori conspiracy), Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh (HSRA) attacked unpopular officials and British property. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged in 1931; their sacrifice made them symbols of national unity and inspired the people.

Explain the formation of the Muslim League in India.

The British encouraged Muslims to form their own political body to weaken national unity. At the Muhammadan Educational Conference at Dacca, Nawab Salimullah Khan proposed it, and the All India Muslim League was founded on 30 December 1906 with the Aga Khan as President, to protect Muslim rights and represent them to the government. It is called the first fruit of Divide and Rule.

la: Why did Lord Curzon partition Bengal in 1905? How did Indians respond to it, and what does their reaction tell us about the spirit of nationalism at that time?

Why: Curzon said it was to improve administration, but the real aim was 'Divide and Rule' — to separate Hindus and Muslims and weaken the strong national movement in Bengal. Response: (1) widespread meetings, processions and press campaigns all over India; (2) Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis to each other; (3) the Swadeshi and Boycott movements — foreign goods were boycotted and swadeshi mills, banks and stores set up, with students and women taking part. Spirit: it showed that nationalism had become a mass feeling, that people were united across religions, self-reliant and no longer afraid of repression; the British had to annul the partition in 1911.

or: Why was the rise of radical nationalists considered a turning point in the freedom struggle? Explain their main beliefs and methods.

Turning point: they ended the era of petitions and made the movement a mass struggle involving peasants, workers, students and women. Beliefs: (1) the British were exploiting India and draining its wealth; (2) freedom was a right, not a favour — 'Swaraj is my birthright'; (3) Indians must be self-reliant. Methods: (4) mass protests and criticism of government policy; (5) boycott of foreign goods and use of swadeshi; (6) national education and promotion of Indian industries. Leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.

la: Why was the Quit India Movement launched? Explain its main features.

Why: (1) the Cripps Mission (1942) failed to offer full independence; (2) wartime shortages and unemployment caused discontent; (3) leaders feared Japan would invade India because of the British presence. Features: (4) the Quit India resolution was passed at Bombay on 8 August 1942 with Gandhi's mantra 'Do or Die'; (5) all leaders were arrested on 9 August, so people led the movement themselves — burning government buildings and cutting railway and telegraph lines, with parallel governments in Ballia, Midnapore and Satara; (6) the British crushed it brutally, but it showed that independence was no longer a matter of bargain.
Describe the role of Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army in the freedom struggle.

(1) Bose saw World War II as an opportunity to strike for freedom. (2) He escaped house arrest to Berlin in 1941, where Indians hailed him as 'Netaji' with 'Jai Hind'. (3) On Ras Bihari Bose's invitation he came to East Asia in 1943 and led the Indian Independence League and the INA (Azad Hind Fauj). (4) He gave the cries 'Chalo Dilli' and 'Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga'. (5) The INA hoisted the Indian flag at Kohima in 1944. (6) Though the INA collapsed, its patriotism inspired Indians and shook British confidence in the loyalty of Indian soldiers.
